claims_disputed.claim: AI usage patterns varied across development phases and teams
claims_disputed.reason: The only evidence is Fig. 4, which is figure-only: team means of a weekly self-reported scale where 0 is 'no use' and 1-4 is perceived helpfulness. A team mean of 2 can mean half non-users and half 'very helpful' users, so differences in use cannot be separated from differences in perceived value. There are 3-4 students per team and four teams, no per-week response counts, and no check against the investigation, done and review reports the template stores in the same repositories (Fig. 2). The direction is plausible, but a descriptive self-report of 14 students is weak evidence.

pattern_stance_changes.reason: §3.2 and Fig. 1 make an AI review phase part of the proposed workflow. After implementation the agent checks requirements, coding conventions and the specs.md update, and writes a prioritized review report (functionality, security, code quality, documentation consistency) into docs/reports/review. The instructors' demo ran it. That is a used and proposed component with no isolating comparison, so it is 'introduces'. Low uptake (Fig. 4) does not make it a mere mention.

missed_issues: Weekly one-on-one comprehension checks ran from lec07 onward (§4.3), so they had been in place for two weeks when three of four teams dipped in lec09. §4.3 also reports improvement in both lec08 and lec10, an alternating pattern on 3-4 students per team, and Late-period (lec11-12) gains 'regardless of AI usage'. §5.1's 'As demonstrated in lec09, proactive intervention is effective' picks one swing of an oscillation. Growing familiarity with the team's own codebase explains the late rise equally well.

Fig. 6a cell sizes are never given. Fourteen students split across four AI-usage levels (level 1 is empty) and three periods leaves some cells very small, so 'students at AI level 0 maintained consistently high code comprehension' may rest on one or two students. The 0-3 comprehension scale has no rubric beyond its four labels, and the number of raters per student and inter-rater agreement are not reported (§3.3).

Phase uptake is measured only by self-report (Fig. 4), although the authors mined the same repositories for added LOC (§3.3) and the template stores investigation, done and review reports under docs/reports alongside specs.md and tasks.md (Fig. 2). Whether teams actually wrote an investigation report and a plan before implementing could have been answered from the repositories and was not reported. That is the key question for P38 and P14.

The 2022 'no AI' baseline is an assumption ('we estimate that generative AI was rarely used in 2022', §4.2); there is no AI-use survey for 2022-2024. If the 2022 course followed the 2025 calendar (team phase from mid-November to mid-January, §3.3), its project weeks overlapped the ChatGPT release that §4.2 dates to November 2022. The conclusion (§6) also pools 2024 with 2025 ('students in 2024-2025 adding more lines of code'), which credits a period, not the SDD/agent intervention.
note: I agree with the review's verdict, COI none and all pattern stances except P18, and with its weak or unsupported grades for the throughput, comprehension, 'essential' and template claims. My rigor is 1 against its 2. Every quantitative result is either a historical-cohort LOC comparison in which the 2025 cohort never beats 2024, or a non-significant, unblinded 0-3 rating of 14 students; the merge takes 1. I lower the one moderate claim (usage varied by phase and team) to weak: it rests on figure-only team means of a scale that mixes non-use with perceived helpfulness, and the repositories that could show whether investigation and review reports were written were never counted. I move P18 to introduces because the AI review report is a designed phase of the proposed workflow with its own template folder. The review also misses that weekly comprehension checks were already running in lec07-08 when the lec09 dip happened, which further weakens the paper's 'intervention then recovery' story.
